summary: This document specifies how a child DNS zone can publish a CSYNC record that tells the parental agent it may copy and process certain records from the child zone. The record and changes to it can be used to keep parent-side data in sync with the child.

plainLanguage.summary: When a domain is delegated to a different organisation, the parent zone still holds the nameserver and address records for it. This document lets the child publish a record saying "these are my current nameservers and addresses, please copy them", and defines how the parent must check that before doing so.

questions: how does child zone sync with parent in dns
how does csync update ns records in the parent zone
what are the csync immediate and soaminimum flags
subtitle: Lets a child DNS zone ask its parent to update the delegation records it holds.

tldr.problem: The nameserver records and address records a parent zone holds for a child zone are expected to match the child's own data, but updating them promptly has always been a manual and error-prone chore.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a new CSYNC record, published at the apex of the child zone, that lists which record types the parent should copy and carries flags controlling when and how the copy happens.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from March 2015, updated by RFC 9975, and it gives parent zones a standard, DNSSEC-validated way to take delegation data straight from the child.

facts.label: Example record
facts.value: example.com. 3600 IN CSYNC 66 3 A NS AAAA

today: RFC 7477 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2015. It is updated by RFC 9975 and has not been obsoleted, so the CSYNC record remains the standard way for a child zone to hand its delegation data to its parent.

sections.title: Keeping Delegations in Step
sections.content:
Some resource records in a parent zone are typically expected to be in sync with the source data in the child's zone. The most common records that should match are the nameserver records and any necessary associated address records, also known as glue records. These records are referred to as delegation records.

It has been challenging for operators of child DNS zones to update their delegation records within the parent's set in a timely fashion. Those difficulties may stem from operator laziness as well as from the complexities of maintaining a large number of DNS zones. An automated mechanism for signalling updates greatly eases the child's maintenance burden and improves the robustness of the DNS as a whole.

The document introduces a new resource record type named CSYNC, which indicates which delegation records published by a child DNS operator should be processed by a parental agent and used to update the parent zone's DNS data. The specification was not designed to synchronise DNSSEC security records such as DS RRsets; for that problem the complementary solution in RFC 7344 is intended. Nor does it address how to perform bootstrapping operations, including getting the initial DNSSEC-secured operating environment in place.

The roles are defined at the outset. The child is the entity on record that has the delegation of the domain from the parent, and the parent is the domain in which the child is registered. The child DNS operator maintains and publishes the zone information for the child DNS. The parental agent is the entity that the child has a relationship with, in order to change its delegation information.
sections.plainLanguage: A delegated domain keeps its nameserver list in two places: in the child's own zone and in the parent's. Until now the second copy was updated by hand, and it often went stale.

sections.title: The CSYNC Record and Its Fields
sections.content:
The CSYNC record type carries three parts in its RDATA component: an SOA serial number, a set of flags, and a simple bit list indicating which DNS record types in the child should be processed by the parental agent in order to modify the delegation records in the parent's zone. A child DNS operator who wants a parental agent to perform these steps MUST publish a CSYNC record at the apex of the child zone. Parental agent implementations MAY choose to query child zones for this record and process the record data as indicated by the Type Bit Map field.

Parental agents MUST process the entire set of child data indicated by the Type Bit Map field, that is, all the record types indicated along with all the necessary records to support processing of that type, or else they MUST NOT make any changes to the parental records at all. Errors due to unsupported Type Bit Map bits, or otherwise unusable data, result in no change to the parent zone's delegation information for the child. A parental agent MUST ignore a child's CSYNC RDATA if multiple CSYNC records are found; only a single CSYNC record should ever be present.

The parental agent MUST perform DNSSEC validation of the CSYNC data and MUST perform DNSSEC validation of any data to be copied from the child to the parent. The parent MUST NOT process any data from these records if any validation result indicates anything other than Secure, or if any required data cannot be retrieved successfully.
sections.plainLanguage: The record holds three things: a version number, some flags, and a list of which kinds of records the parent should take. The parent either takes all of them or takes none.

sections.title: The Wire Format
sections.content:
The RDATA of a CSYNC record has an SOA Serial field of 32 bits, a Flags field of 16 bits, and a Type Bit Map field that may continue over further 32-bit words. The Type Bit Map is encoded in the same way as the Type Bit Map field of the NSEC record, as described in Section 4.1.2 of RFC 4034. If a bit has been set that a parental agent implementation does not understand, the parental agent MUST NOT act upon the record: it must not simply copy the data, and it must understand the semantics associated with any bit that is set to one.

The SOA Serial field holds a copy of the 32-bit SOA serial number from the child zone. If the soaminimum flag is set, parental agents querying children's authoritative servers MUST NOT act on data from zones advertising an SOA serial number less than this value, using the proper less-than logic of RFC 1982. If the flag is not set, parental agents MUST ignore the value, and clients can set it to anything, such as zero. A child SHOULD update the SOA Serial field every time the data referenced by the CSYNC record changes, and MAY choose to keep it equal to the current SOA serial number. A child using the soaminimum flag must not increment its SOA serial number by more than 2^16 within the period a parent might wait between polling.

The Flags field holds 16 boolean flags. Two are defined here: bit 0 is immediate, and bit 1 is soaminimum. The remaining flags are reserved for future specifications, and undefined flags MUST be set to zero by publishers. A parental agent MUST NOT process a CSYNC record that contains a one in a flag it does not know or does not support. In the presentation format the SOA Serial and Flags fields are integers, and the Type Bit Map is written as a sequence of record type mnemonics, with the TYPE representation of RFC 3597 used when a mnemonic is not known.
sections.plainLanguage: The record is a version number, two flag bits, and a bitmap of record types. A parent that meets an unknown flag or an unknown bitmap bit refuses to act at all.

sections.title: How the Parental Agent Processes a Record
sections.content:
The CSYNC record and its associated data must be processed as an all-or-nothing operation. If a parental agent fails to query successfully for any of the required records, the whole operation MUST be aborted, and a query resulting in no records existing, as proven by NSEC or NSEC3, counts as successful.

The parental agent MAY process the record immediately if the immediate flag is set. If that flag is not set, the parental agent MUST NOT act until the zone administrator approves the operation through an out-of-band mechanism, such as pushing a button in a web interface. It may also choose not to process the record immediately even when the flag is set, for instance if it requires approval out of band. How that approval is done is outside the scope of the document and specific to the parental agent.

The processing sequence has four steps. First, query for the child zone's SOA record. Second, query for the child zone's CSYNC record. Third, query for the child's data records as required by the CSYNC record's Type Bit Map field. If any of the records being queried are not authoritative within the child zone but in a grandchild or deeper, SOA queries must also be made for the grandchildren, which means the agent has to work out where the zone cuts occur; because of that extra complexity, parental agents MAY choose not to support the protocol with children that use records authoritative in grandchildren. Fourth, query for the collected SOA records again, starting with the deepest and ending with the child's own SOA.

If the SOA records from the first, middle and last steps for a given zone have different serial numbers, for example because the zone was edited and republished in between, the CSYNC record obtained SHOULD NOT be processed, and the operation MAY be restarted or retried later. If the soaminimum flag is set and the serial numbers are equal but less than the CSYNC record's SOA Serial field, the record MUST NOT be processed. If the agent keeps state and the serial number is less than the last time a CSYNC record was processed, or the CSYNC record's SOA Serial field is less than that of the last one, the record SHOULD NOT be processed. If any failure occurs while obtaining the required data, or DNSSEC fails to validate all of the returned data as secure, the record MUST NOT be processed.
sections.plainLanguage: The parent reads the child's version number, fetches the records named in the bitmap, then reads the version number again. If anything changed in between, or if a single query fails, nothing is updated.

sections.title: Which Records Get Copied
sections.content:
The NS type flag means the NS records from the child zone should be copied into the parent's delegation information for the child. NS records found in the child's zone should be copied verbatim, with the exception of the TTL, for which the parent may want a different value, and the set published in the parent should match exactly. If the child has published a new NS record within its set, that record should be added to the parent zone, and if the parent's delegation records contain records removed from the child's NS set, they should be removed from the parent's set as well. Parental agents MAY refuse to perform NS updates if the replacement records fail to meet the NS record policies required by the parent zone, such as requiring every child zone to have at least two NS records. They MUST NOT perform NS updates if no NS records are returned in a query, as verified by DNSSEC denial-of-existence protection, a situation that should never happen unless the child nameservers are misconfigured. It is permissible for a child's nameserver to return a CSYNC record that removes the queried nameserver itself from the future NS or address set.

The A and AAAA type flags mean the address glue records for in-bailiwick NS records within the child zone should be copied verbatim, again with the exception of the TTL, into the parent's delegation information. Queries should be sent to determine the addresses for each NS record in the child's NS set that is in bailiwick. Only matching types should be queried: if the AAAA bit is not set, the AAAA records in the parent's delegation should remain as they are. If a given address type is set and the child's zone contains no data for that type, as proven by NSEC or NSEC3, the result in the parent should be an empty set. However, if the result of processing would leave no glue records present in the parent zone for any of the in-bailiwick NS records, the parent MUST NOT update the glue address records, because that would leave the parent and child relationship without any address linkage.

The procedure for querying A and AAAA records MUST occur after the NS procedure, so that the right set of NS records is used: for a CSYNC record with the NS bit set, the NS set used is the one pulled from the child while processing; for a record without the NS bit set, the existing NS records in the parent are used to decide which address records to update.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the nameserver list and the addresses of servers inside the child's own domain are copied. The parent never ends up with an empty address list for a delegation that has servers.

sections.title: Running It in Practice
sections.content:
There is no inline mechanism for a parental agent to report errors to the operators of child zones, so error reporting must be out of band, such as through a web console or over email. Parental agents should at least log the errors they encounter. A child operator using the immediate flag who fails to see an update within the agent's operational window should look at the agent's error log to find out why.

Parental agents poll child nameservers for CSYNC records and related data. They MAY perform best-possible verification by querying all the NS records for available data to determine which has the most recent SOA and CSYNC version, since in practice they will not all be equal because of synchronisation delays and transfer failures. An agent may offer a configuration interface allowing child operators to specify which nameserver should be treated as the master to send data queries to, which could be a hidden master rather than one of the publicly listed nameservers. Agents with many clients may offer a programmatic interface so that children can indicate that new CSYNC records are available rather than being polled constantly.

A child wishing to phase out a nameserver needs to publish the CSYNC record that removes it and then wait for the parental agent to process the published record before turning off the service, because the child cannot control which nameserver in the existing NS set the agent may choose to query.

When a zone contains NS records whose domain name falls outside the zone itself, there is no way for the parent to safely update the associated glue records. The child DNS operator MAY indicate that the NS records should be synchronized and MAY set the address flags as well, but the parent will only update those glue records that are below the child's delegation point. Children deploying NS records pointing to names inside their own children should ensure the grandchildren's glue records are properly set before publishing the CSYNC record.

Parental agents that support CSYNC processing SHOULD publicly document that they support it, which Type Bit Map bits they support, the frequency with which they poll clients and whether that is configurable, whether they support the immediate flag, whether they poll a single nameserver, a configured list or all the advertised nameservers, whether they support SOA serial number caching, where errors are published, and whether they support sending queries to a hidden master. Children MAY remove the CSYNC record once they notice the parent has published the required records, which removes the need for the parent to keep querying for the CSYNC record and all the corresponding records.
sections.plainLanguage: Failures are reported out of band, in logs. The parent has to be polled, and the child has to wait for the parent to catch up before turning a server off.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The specification requires the use of DNSSEC in order to determine that the data being updated was not modified by third parties. Parental agents implementing CSYNC processing MUST ensure all DNS transactions are validated by DNSSEC as secure. Clients deploying CSYNC MUST ensure their zones are signed, current and properly linked to the parent zone with a DS record pointing at an appropriate DNSKEY of the child's zone.

The specification does not address how to bootstrap the initial DNSSEC-secured operating environment, and it was not designed to synchronise DNSSEC security records such as DS pointers, or the CSYNC record itself. Implementations of this protocol MUST NOT use it to synchronise DS records, DNSKEY material, CDS records, CDNSKEY records or CSYNC records, and future documents extending the protocol MUST NOT offer the ability to do so. For that, the complementary solution in RFC 7344 maintains security delegation information.

To ensure that an older CSYNC record using the soaminimum flag cannot be replayed to revert values, the SOA serial number MUST NOT be incremented by more than 2^16 during the lifetime of the signature window of the associated RRSIGs signing the SOA and CSYNC records. This holds regardless of whether the increment causes the 32-bit serial number field to wrap.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything has to be signed, so the parent can tell the child did not change its mind halfway through, and the protocol deliberately cannot be used to move the signed delegation records themselves.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The document defines a new DNS resource record type named CSYNC, and IANA has assigned the code point 62 in the Resource Record TYPEs sub-registry of the Domain Name System Parameters registry for it.

A sub-registry called the Child Synchronization (CSYNC) Flags registry has been created and is maintained by IANA. It holds a set of single-bit flags for use in the CSYNC record within the 16-bit Flags field, so a maximum of 16 flags may be defined. The initial assignments are bit 0, immediate, which asks for the CSYNC record to be processed immediately, and bit 1, soaminimum, which requires a SOA serial number greater than the one specified. A Standards Action is required for the assignment of any new flag value.
sections.plainLanguage: The record type gets the number 62, and the two flags are numbered 0 and 1 with room for fourteen more.

fields.name: SOA Serial
fields.desc: A copy of the child zone's 32-bit SOA serial number.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Bit 0 is immediate, bit 1 is soaminimum. The rest are reserved.

fields.name: Type Bit Map
fields.desc: First part of the bitmap of record types to process.

fields.name: Type Bit Map (continued)
fields.desc: The bitmap continues in further 32-bit words.

viz.caption: THE EXAMPLE CSYNC RECORD AND ITS WIRE FORM (RFC 7477, SECTION 2.1.3)

data.title: Example CSYNC record
data.code:
example.com. 3600 IN CSYNC 66 3 A NS AAAA

0x00 0x00 0x00 0x42             (SOA Serial)
0x00 0x03                       (Flags = immediate | soaminimum)
0x00 0x04 0x60 0x00 0x00 0x08   (Type Bit Map)

messages.label: QUERY SOA
messages.note: Step 1: note the child's serial number.

messages.label: QUERY CSYNC
messages.note: Step 2: read the record and its bitmap.

messages.label: QUERY DATA RECORDS
messages.note: Step 3: fetch the records named in the bitmap.

messages.label: QUERY SOA AGAIN
messages.note: Step 4: check that nothing changed in the meantime.

items.label: IMMEDIATE
items.desc: Process this CSYNC record immediately rather than waiting for approval.

items.label: SOAMINIMUM
items.desc: Require the zone's SOA serial number to be greater than the one specified.
